title: Key West, Florida
excerpt: A charter bus to Key West means 113 miles of Overseas Highway and 42 bridges. Vehicle choice, Old Town access limits, and how to plan the drive.

heroImage.alt: A motorcoach crossing one of the long causeway bridges on the Overseas Highway between the Florida Keys under a bright sky

extraImage.alt: Passengers stepping off a charter bus near the waterfront in Old Town Key West late in the afternoon

body.text: There is no ordinary way to arrive in Key West. A charter bus to Key West means driving the Overseas Highway, roughly 113 miles of US-1 running from Florida City down to the southernmost point of the continental United States, crossing 42 bridges along the way. It is one of the genuinely great American drives, and it is the single strongest argument for putting a group on one vehicle rather than splitting into cars.

On a coach, everybody sees it. Nobody is watching the road instead of the water, nobody is checking a navigation app, and nobody misses the Seven Mile Bridge because they were looking for the next turn. That is a real difference, not a marketing line.

Plan for around four hours from Miami in good conditions, and be honest with your group that conditions are not always good. US-1 through the Keys is largely a two-lane road with limited passing. A single incident, a bridge opening, or heavy weekend traffic can add an hour or more. Groups that budget four hours and treat anything faster as a bonus have a much better day than groups that promise three.

items: From Miami: roughly 160 miles, about four hours with a stop.
From Fort Lauderdale: add around forty minutes to the Miami timing.
From Orlando: this is a full travel day of roughly seven to eight hours. Most groups break it with an overnight rather than attempting it in one push.
Build in at least one proper stop. Islamorada and Marathon both have places a coach can pull in comfortably, and a group that has been sitting for two hours will thank you.

body.text: Old Town is the constraint nobody plans for

This is the practical warning worth reading twice. Key West's historic district was laid out long before motorcoaches existed. The streets in Old Town are narrow, many are one-way, and Duval Street in particular is not somewhere a full-size coach belongs. Large-vehicle access and parking are genuinely limited across the island.

In practice this means your itinerary should treat the coach as a shuttle to and from the island rather than a vehicle that follows you around it. Plan a drop point, then move around Old Town on foot, by trolley, or by the local transit that is built for those streets. Old Town is compact and extremely walkable, which is why this works well once you stop fighting it. Talk to your coordinator early about where your group will be set down and collected, because that decision shapes the whole day.

items: Mallory Square at sunset. The Sunset Celebration with its street performers is the closest thing the island has to a nightly civic ritual, and it is free.
The Ernest Hemingway Home and Museum, complete with the descendants of the writer's six-toed cats. It is small, so large groups should plan to enter in waves.
The Harry S. Truman Little White House, which is more genuinely interesting than most visitors expect and works well for adult and history-focused groups.
Dry Tortugas National Park, reachable by ferry or seaplane. This is a full day and needs booking well ahead, but it is the standout excursion for groups with the time.
The Southernmost Point buoy, where the queue moves slowly. Send the group in shifts rather than standing in a block of thirty.

body.text: Picking the right charter bus for a Keys trip
Vehicle choice matters more here than on most routes, because you are combining a long highway leg with a very constrained destination.

items: For 40 or more passengers, a full-size coach from our [motor coach fleet](/fleet/motor-coaches) is the comfortable answer for the Overseas Highway. Reclining seats, climate control, luggage bays and an onboard restroom matter a great deal on a four-hour drive.
For 20 to 32 passengers, a [mini bus](/fleet/mini-buses) is noticeably easier to place on the island and simpler to maneuver on the narrower stretches of US-1.
For 10 to 14 passengers, a [sprinter van](/fleet/sprinter-vans) gives the most flexibility of all and can reach places a coach simply cannot.
Whatever the size, confirm the restroom situation before you leave. On this particular route it is not a luxury question.

body.text: Winter and early spring, roughly December through April, are the most reliable months and also the busiest. Summer is hot, humid and quiet, with genuine bargains available if your group tolerates heat. Hurricane season runs from the first of June through the end of November, and it deserves real respect in the Keys specifically, because US-1 is the only road out. Evacuation orders for the Keys are issued early and taken seriously. If you are travelling in September or October, build flexibility into your bookings and keep an eye on forecasts.
Fantasy Fest in late October and the winter holidays are the two periods when accommodation and access are hardest. Plan those dates many months ahead or avoid them entirely.

items: Confirm your drop-off and pickup points before travel day, not on it.
A day trip from Miami is possible but long. Two nights on the island is a far better trip.
Tell your coordinator if Dry Tortugas is in the plan, since ferry departure times are fixed and early.
Sun protection is not optional. There is very little shade at the popular stops.
